# Gelatox

> A one-page buyer's guide to Gelatox, a skin, hair and nail gummy supplement sold as 60 gummies per jar and chewed two a day. Written for readers in the United States at https://gelatox-org.vercel.app/. Orders complete on the official checkout. Last reviewed 17 November 2026.

Gelatox swaps the capsule for a gummy and the botanical blend for a run of B-vitamins, biotin foremost. The seller presents it as a 100% natural formula that accelerates cell renewal, reinforces the skin's moisture barrier and supplies antioxidants against free radicals. A serving is two gummies, taken roughly 30 minutes before a morning or afternoon meal with a full glass of water, so a 60-gummy jar runs 30 days. Six nutrients are named on the official listing — biotin, vitamin B12 as methylcobalamin, vitamin B6 as pyridoxine hydrochloride, folate, pantothenic acid as d-calcium pantothenate, and vitamin A — and not one of them carries a microgram, milligram or Daily Value figure; the Supplement Facts panel appears online only as an image, and no other ingredients or allergens are listed. Three packages are sold: two bottles at $79 each ($158 plus a postage charge the seller never names, about $2.63 a day before it), three bottles at $69 each ($207 posted free, about $2.30 a day) and six bottles at $49 each ($294 posted free, about $1.63 a day). Six digital guides, which the seller values at $358 together, attach to the three and six bottle orders. Every order carries a 60-day Results or Refund Guarantee. Charged once, with nothing recurring. Sold to adults 18 and over.

## Sources cited on this page

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: biotin](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/biotin-consumer/): states there is little scientific evidence that biotin supplements improve hair, skin or nails, and warns that high intakes can cause false results in some laboratory tests including thyroid hormone testing.
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: vitamin A](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-Consumer/): recommended intakes and upper limits for vitamin A, relevant because no amount is published for this product.
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: what you need to know](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/): a plain-language primer on what dietary supplements are and how they are regulated.
- [MedlinePlus: skin, hair and nails](https://medlineplus.gov/skinhairandnails.html): consumer background on hair loss, nail disease and skin conditions, and when to seek a diagnosis.
- [NIH News in Health: keep your skin healthy](https://newsinhealth.nih.gov/2015/11/keep-your-skin-healthy): washing, moisturising and sun-protection basics from the National Institutes of Health.
- [FDA: dietary supplements](https://www.fda.gov/food/dietary-supplements): supplements fall under food law rather than medicines law in the United States, with no pre-market approval.
- [FTC: health claims](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/health-claims): the advertising rules a supplement health claim has to meet.
